title: From a Bent Bundle to a Pushing Cell

scenes.tts: How does one cell push on a sound wave, many thousands of times a second?
scenes.visual: Title card: From a Bent Bundle to a Pushing Cell. One outer hair cell beside a fast sine wave. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: How does one cell push on a sound wave, many thousands of times a second?

scenes.tts: The chain has five links. Sound bends the hair bundle back and forth. Bending toward the tallest stereocilia opens more transduction channels.
scenes.visual: Numbered chain at the side. Link 1 lights: the hair bundle tips one way, then the other. Link 2 lights: channels at the bundle tips open more as it tips toward the tall side, and fewer as it tips back.
scenes.narration: The chain has five links. Sound bends the hair bundle back and forth. Bending toward the tallest stereocilia opens more transduction channels.

scenes.tts: Current flows in, so the voltage rises and falls with the bundle. The voltage moves charge inside prestin, which changes shape.
scenes.visual: Link 3 lights: a current arrow into the cell, a voltage trace that rises and falls. Link 4 lights: prestin dots in the lateral wall shift shape.
scenes.narration: Current flows in, so the voltage rises and falls with the bundle. The voltage moves charge inside prestin, which changes shape.

scenes.tts: The cell shortens and lengthens in step, and pushes on the organ of Corti.
scenes.visual: Link 5 lights: the cell shortens as the voltage rises and lengthens as it falls, pushing on the structure above and below it.
scenes.narration: The cell shortens and lengthens in step, and pushes on the organ of Corti.

scenes.tts: Why voltage? A twenty kilohertz tone completes a cycle every fifty microseconds.
scenes.caption: Why voltage? A 20 kHz tone completes a cycle every 50 microseconds.
scenes.visual: A clock tick for one cycle. On screen: 20 kHz, one cycle = 50 microseconds.
scenes.narration: Why voltage? A 20 kHz tone completes a cycle every 50 microseconds.

scenes.tts: An amplifier working on every cycle cannot wait on a slow chemical step, such as A T P hydrolysis.
scenes.caption: An amplifier working on every cycle cannot wait on a slow chemical step, such as ATP hydrolysis.
scenes.visual: A slow chemical-step icon (ATP) lags behind the fast cycle, crossed out. Prestin and the voltage trace move in step.
scenes.narration: An amplifier working on every cycle cannot wait on a slow chemical step, such as ATP hydrolysis.

scenes.tts: Voltage has limits too. The membrane smooths fast voltage changes. In simple estimates, its cutoff lies far below the highest frequencies basal cells amplify. How much that limits the amplifier is still argued.
scenes.visual: The voltage swing shrinks as the input frequency rises. Labels: membrane resistance and capacitance; simple estimate, cutoff far below high frequencies; still argued (Altoè and Shera, 2023).
scenes.narration: Voltage has limits too. The membrane smooths fast voltage changes. In simple estimates, its cutoff lies far below the highest frequencies basal cells amplify. How much that limits the amplifier is still argued.

scenes.tts: How can you watch prestin's charge move? Measure capacitance, the charge moved per change in voltage.
scenes.visual: A voltage-clamp pipette touches a cell. On screen: C = dQ/dV. Axes: charge against voltage.
scenes.narration: How can you watch prestin's charge move? Measure capacitance, the charge moved per change in voltage.

scenes.tts: In the simplest model, each prestin flips between two states, and voltage tilts the odds. So its charge moves along an S-shaped curve, mostly near its midpoint.
scenes.visual: Two prestin states flicker; a voltage slider tilts the balance. An S-shaped charge curve draws on the axes, midpoint marked. A corner label, kept on screen through the worked example: two-state equilibrium model, T = 295 K.
scenes.narration: In the simplest model, each prestin flips between two states, and voltage tilts the odds. So its charge moves along an S-shaped curve, mostly near its midpoint.

scenes.tts: The slope of an S peaks at its middle. So the extra capacitance is a bell, called nonlinear capacitance.
scenes.visual: A tangent slides along the S; beneath it a bell draws as the slope, peaking under the midpoint. Label: nonlinear capacitance (NLC). The bell is labelled: nonlinear component, normalized to its own peak.
scenes.narration: The slope of an S peaks at its middle. So the extra capacitance is a bell, called nonlinear capacitance.

scenes.tts: Its steepness is set by z, the effective charge that moves per prestin.
scenes.visual: Label: z, effective valence. The S and bell shown together.
scenes.narration: Its steepness is set by z, the effective charge that moves per prestin.

scenes.tts: Predict. If z doubles, does the bell get wider or narrower?
scenes.visual: Two empty bell outlines side by side: z = 0.70 and z = 1.40. Text: Predict.
scenes.narration: Predict. If z doubles, does the bell get wider or narrower?

scenes.tts: Narrower. A larger z makes the S steeper. The width of the bell scales as one over z.
scenes.visual: The S steepens; the bell narrows. Half-height widths on screen: about 128 mV at z = 0.70, about 64 mV at z = 1.40. Width scales as 1/z. Corner label: two-state equilibrium model, T = 295 K.
scenes.narration: Narrower. A larger z makes the S steeper. The width of the bell scales as one over z.

scenes.tts: Take the gerbil fit. At fifty millivolts above the midpoint, about eighty percent of prestin is in the contracted state. The bell there is sixty-four percent of its peak.
scenes.caption: Take the gerbil fit. At 50 mV above the midpoint, about 80% of prestin is in the contracted state. The bell there is 64% of its peak.
scenes.visual: Bell with Vh = -112 mV; a marker at -62 mV. On screen: z = 0.70, f = 0.798, NLC = 4f(1 - f) = 0.64 of its own peak. Small labels: two-state model, 295 K, normalized NLC, linear capacitance excluded.
scenes.narration: Take the gerbil fit. At 50 mV above the midpoint, about 80% of prestin is in the contracted state. The bell there is 64% of its peak.

scenes.tts: This reads charge movement, not the force or power a hair cell produces.
scenes.visual: Label: charge movement, yes; force or power, no.
scenes.narration: This reads charge movement, not the force or power a hair cell produces.

scenes.tts: Structures of purified prestin suggest an area motor. But each is a candidate end state, not a working motor.
scenes.visual: A schematic prestin dimer in a membrane, its footprint growing and shrinking. Two frozen snapshots labelled chloride and salicylate. Label: end states, not a movie.
scenes.narration: Structures of purified prestin suggest an area motor. But each is a candidate end state, not a working motor.

scenes.tts: Is the motor needed? In a prestin knock-in mouse, transduction and cell mechanics were normal. Yet amplification was lost.
scenes.visual: A mouse icon labelled prestin knock-in. Ticks: transduction normal, cell mechanics normal. A cross on amplification.
scenes.narration: Is the motor needed? In a prestin knock-in mouse, transduction and cell mechanics were normal. Yet amplification was lost.

scenes.tts: So the cell body's motility is necessary. In an excised frog organ, a hair bundle can also add energy.
scenes.visual: Label: somatic motility is necessary (Dallos and colleagues, 2008). A frog bundle icon appears, labelled excised bullfrog sacculus.
scenes.narration: So the cell body's motility is necessary. In an excised frog organ, a hair bundle can also add energy.

scenes.tts: How the work is split between bundle and cell body in mammals has not been established.
scenes.visual: A frog bundle icon with a question mark beside a mammalian outer hair cell.
scenes.narration: How the work is split between bundle and cell body in mammals has not been established.

scenes.tts: Take this with you. Bundle, channel, voltage, prestin, push. The bell is the motor's electrical fingerprint.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the five-link chain in a row, and the bell beneath it.
scenes.narration: Take this with you. Bundle, channel, voltage, prestin, push. The bell is the motor's electrical fingerprint.
